draft.title: Literal and implied meaning
card: This is what a text says on the surface. It is the plain meaning of the words.
This is what a reader works out from details the text does not state outright. The reader infers it.
Example: "I'm fine," said Leo, and he slammed the door. Literally, Leo says he is fine. The slammed door implies he is angry or upset.
To find implied meaning, look at actions, tone and word choices, and ask what they suggest beyond the words themselves.
draft.remember: Literal is what the words say. Implied is what the details suggest.

a.q: Priya says, "I don't mind," but she stares at the floor and her voice shakes. What is the implied meaning?
opts: She is actually upset about something
She is looking at the floor for fun
She does not mind at all
She has dropped something on the floor
a.why: Her words literally say she does not mind. Her stare and shaky voice imply she is upset. The option that she does not mind repeats only the literal meaning and ignores the details.
a.clue: Look at what she does, not only what she says.

b.q: Mia writes that Sam reached the stop just as the bus left. He then looked at his watch and sighed. Which is an implied meaning?
opts: Sam is frustrated that he missed the bus
The bus left from the stop
b.why: The text never says Sam is frustrated, but the missed bus and his sigh suggest it. The other three options state events the text says directly, so they are literal meanings.
b.clue: Which option is not stated directly in the text?

a.best: She is actually upset about something

b.best: Sam is frustrated that he missed the bus
